turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell found it astonishing that Mr. Worthing had been so careless with his information, and she insisted that he produce a reference to confirm the ownership of his house in Belgrave Square.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he was unable to provide a reference, as he had recently moved to the area and did not know many people.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell turned to Gwendolen with a stern expression, saying, 'Gwendolen, I fear that your prospective husband is not quite the gentleman we had hoped for.'

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen, who had been waiting patiently in the carriage, had a sudden urge to intervene in the conversation.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he was a gentleman of independent means, and he had always been careful with his finances, as a gentleman should.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that his claim of being a gentleman of independent means was hardly reassuring, given the lack of concrete evidence to support it.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he was a man of simple tastes and modest means, and that he had always tried to live within his means and not to indulge in any lavish spending.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell expressed her skepticism, 'I highly doubt, Mr. Worthing, that a man who has been living with a lady in such close quarters for five years without the benefit of marriage is truly a gentleman of refined morals.'

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Told Lady Bracknell that he understood her concerns, but he had always tried to be a responsible and reliable partner to Gwendolen, and he hoped that his actions would speak for themselves.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen called out to the driver to bring the carriage around, her voice loud and insistent, indicating her growing impatience with the proceedings

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he had always been open and honest with Gwendolen, and that their relationship was built on trust and mutual respect.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell turned to Gwendolen with a disapproving glance, asked Gwendolen to inform her immediately of any potential objections to the engagement, and warned Gwendolen that a decision must be made soon, as the waiting was becoming most tiresome.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen called out to her mother, her voice firm and determined, saying she had no intention of being delayed by Lady Bracknell's questioning for a moment longer.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell insisted that Mr. Worthing's family history and background were of the utmost importance, and that she would not allow her daughter to marry a man whose personal circumstances were shrouded in mystery.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that his mother was a ward in a lunatic asylum, and that he had been told she was dead, but he was afraid to reveal the truth to Gwendolen as he was afraid it might cause her distress

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Mr. Worthing that his candor was commendable, but that a mere ward in a lunatic asylum was hardly a suitable maternal figure for a young woman of Gwendolen's standing.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack asked, somewhat hesitantly, if his mother's past was the only concern Lady Bracknell had about his suitability as a husband for Gwendolen

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell turned her gaze upon Jack with an air of distaste, telling him that his family history, though perhaps unusual, was hardly the only consideration in determining his suitability as a husband for a young woman of Gwendolen's standing and connections.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he could hardly be expected to reveal all the details of his mother's past, and that he hoped Lady Bracknell would consider his own character and intentions in determining his suitability as a husband for Gwendolen

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that she would not consider his character and intentions until his family history was fully disclosed and explained.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell that she was engaged to Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Gwendolen and Mr. Worthing to pardon her, as they were not engaged to anyone. She explained that when they did become engaged, she or Mr. Worthing's father, if his health permitted, would inform them of the fact. An engagement should come as a surprise to a young girl, and it was hardly a matter she could arrange for herself. While she was making inquiries, Gwendolen would wait for her below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen called out to Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen to wait for her in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen replied to Lady Bracknell that she would wait for her.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Mr. Worthing to take a seat.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack stood tall, his eyes locked on Lady Bracknell, and said that he preferred to remain standing, rather than take a seat.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell informed Mr. Worthing that he was not on her list of eligible young men, although she had the same list as the Duchess of Bolton. However, she was willing to enter his name if his answers were satisfactory. She asked him if he smoked.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing admitted to Lady Bracknell that he smoked.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing smoked. She believed that a man should have an occupation. There were too many idle men in London. She asked Mr. Worthing how old he was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he was twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that twenty-nine was a good age to get married. She believed that a man who wanted to get married should know either everything or nothing. She asked Mr. Worthing which category he fell into.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that he knew nothing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing knew nothing. She believed that ignorance was a delicate and exotic fruit that should not be tampered with. She stated that education was unsound and produced no effect in England. If it did, it would be a danger to the upper classes. She asked Mr. Worthing about his income.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his income was between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing if his income came from land or investments.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that his income came from investments.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that Mr. Worthing's income was satisfactory. She stated that land was no longer a profit or pleasure, but rather a means of gaining position and losing it. She asked Mr. Worthing about his country house.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he had a country house with some land, but he did not depend on it for his income. In fact, the poachers were the only ones who made anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing how many bedrooms his country house had. She also asked if he had a town house, as a girl like Gwendolen could not be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he owned a house in Belgrave Square, but it was let by the year to Lady Bloxham.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing who Lady Bloxham was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack observed that Lady Bracknell went out very little, and that she was a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing what number his house in Belgrave Square was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his house was number 149.
